title: Design a payment gateway for a bank. Explain the end-to-end architecture, how you guarantee a payment is processed exactly once, how you keep money consistent across services, and how you make the system resilient and observable at scale.

s1_definition.profdef: A payment gateway is a system that accepts a payment request, validates it, moves money between accounts reliably, and notifies downstream systems. At scale it is built as stateless, horizontally scaled services behind an API gateway, uses idempotency keys to guarantee each payment is applied exactly once despite retries, coordinates the multi-step money movement with a Saga pattern and compensating transactions, publishes events through the transactional outbox pattern to Kafka for asynchronous consumers, and is made resilient with circuit breakers and retries and observable with metrics, logs, and traces.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the payment gateway as the central money-transfer department at National Bank of India. When Rajesh asks to send money to Priya, a guard at the door (API gateway) checks his ID and that he is not flooding the counter. A clerk checks whether this exact request was already processed (idempotency), so if Rajesh accidentally clicks "Pay" twice, the money moves only once. The transfer happens in careful steps — take money from Rajesh, give it to Priya, record the settlement — and if any step fails, the department undoes the earlier steps so no money is lost (Saga with compensation). Finally, the department drops a note in the mailroom (Kafka) so the SMS team, the analytics team, and the reconciliation team can each pick it up and act independently.
s1_definition.oneliner: A payment gateway moves money through validated, idempotent, Saga-coordinated steps, publishes events via an outbox to Kafka, and stays resilient with circuit breakers and observable with metrics, logs, and traces.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A payment gateway is a system that accepts a payment request, validates it, moves money between accounts reliably, and notifies downstream systems. At scale it is built as stateless, horizontally scaled services behind an API gateway, uses idempotency keys to guarantee each payment is applied exactly once despite retries, coordinates the multi-step money movement with a Saga pattern and compensating transactions, publishes events through the transactional outbox pattern to Kafka for asynchronous consumers, and is made resilient with circuit breakers and retries and observable with metrics, logs, and traces.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the payment gateway as the central money-transfer department at National Bank of India. When Rajesh asks to send money to Priya, a guard at the door (API gateway) checks his ID and that he is not flooding the counter. A clerk checks whether this exact request was already processed (idempotency), so if Rajesh accidentally clicks "Pay" twice, the money moves only once. The transfer happens in careful steps — take money from Rajesh, give it to Priya, record the settlement — and if any step fails, the department undoes the earlier steps so no money is lost (Saga with compensation). Finally, the department drops a note in the mailroom (Kafka) so the SMS team, the analytics team, and the reconciliation team can each pick it up and act independently.

**One line to remember:** A payment gateway moves money through validated, idempotent, Saga-coordinated steps, publishes events via an outbox to Kafka, and stays resilient with circuit breakers and observable with metrics, logs, and traces.

sections.s2_technical:
The request enters through an API gateway that handles TLS termination, authentication, and rate limiting, so unauthenticated or abusive traffic never reaches the core. Behind it the payment service is stateless and horizontally scaled, meaning you can run many identical copies and a load balancer spreads traffic across them; because they hold no session state, any instance can serve any request.

The single most important correctness property is idempotency. The client sends an idempotency key with each payment, and the service stores that key in Redis mapped to the result. If the same key arrives again — because the client retried after a timeout — the service returns the stored result instead of moving money a second time. In code this is a check like `if (redis.exists(idempotencyKey)) return redis.get(idempotencyKey);` before doing any work. This is what prevents double-charging Rajesh when his phone retries a request it thought failed.

Moving money touches multiple services, so you cannot rely on a single database transaction. Instead you use the Saga pattern: a sequence of local transactions where each step has a compensating action. Step one debits Rajesh, step two credits Priya, step three records settlement. If crediting Priya fails, the Saga runs the compensation for step one and re-credits Rajesh, so the system is never left with money missing. Each service call is wrapped in a circuit breaker and retry so a transient downstream failure does not fail the whole payment.

To tell the rest of the world what happened without tight coupling, you use the transactional outbox pattern. In the same database transaction that records the payment, you also insert an event row into an outbox table. A relay process reads the outbox and publishes to a Kafka topic such as `payment-events`. This guarantees the event is published if and only if the payment was committed, avoiding the dual-write problem where the database and Kafka could disagree. Consumers subscribe to the topic: a notification consumer sends SMS and email, an analytics consumer updates dashboards, and a reconciliation consumer matches records at end of day.

For data, PostgreSQL stores the authoritative account and payment tables, sharded by account id so one database does not become a bottleneck, with read replicas serving heavy reporting queries. Redis stores idempotency keys, rate-limit counters, and session data. A senior-level nuance is that consistency here is a deliberate choice: money movement is strongly consistent within each local transaction, while notifications and analytics are eventually consistent through Kafka, which is the right trade-off because a slightly delayed SMS is fine but a lost debit is not. Observability ties it together with Prometheus and Grafana for metrics, structured logs in ELK, distributed tracing with correlation ids, and PagerDuty alerts when latency or error rates breach thresholds.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, Rajesh sends Rs.50,000 rent to Priya through the mobile app. We need this to be correct even when the network is unreliable.

Problem 1 — Rajesh's phone loses signal after tapping Pay, so the app retries the request. Without protection, the bank would debit Rajesh twice. This is exactly what idempotency solves: the service remembers the idempotency key and returns the first result instead of moving money again.

Problem 2 — Debiting Rajesh succeeds, but crediting Priya fails because her account service is momentarily down. Without care, Rajesh loses money that never reaches Priya. This is exactly what a Saga with compensation solves: the failed credit triggers a re-credit of Rajesh so the system returns to a consistent state.

Problem 3 — Once the transfer succeeds, the SMS team, the analytics team, and the reconciliation team all need to know, but the payment must not wait for them. This is exactly what the outbox-plus-Kafka pattern solves: the payment commits with an event in the same transaction, and consumers pick it up asynchronously.

The code will contain an `Account` class, an `IdempotencyStore` (a stand-in for Redis), a `PaymentService` whose `transfer` method checks idempotency and runs a Saga of debit-then-credit with compensation on failure, and an `EventOutbox` that records events to be relayed to Kafka. A `PaymentGatewayDemo` main class shows a successful transfer, a duplicate request returning the cached result, and a failed credit triggering compensation.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, Rs.1,000,000), Priya (CUR3001, Rs.250,000), a rent transfer of Rs.50,000, and an idempotency key "IDEM-RENT-001".

Step 1: The first `transfer` call checks the idempotency store for key "IDEM-RENT-001". It is not present, so the service proceeds with the Saga.

Step 2: Saga step one debits Rajesh by 50,000, so his balance changes from 1,000,000 to 950,000. This is a local change recorded immediately.

Step 3: Saga step two credits Priya by 50,000, so her balance changes from 250,000 to 300,000. If this had thrown, the service would have re-credited Rajesh to undo step one, leaving both balances unchanged.

Step 4: The service generates payment id "TXF-1", stores the result "TXF-1:COMPLETED" under the idempotency key, and records an event in the outbox in the same logical transaction. It returns the result.

Step 5: The second `transfer` call uses the same idempotency key. This time the store already contains "TXF-1:COMPLETED", so the service returns that cached result immediately without touching any balance. Rajesh is debited only once, which is the whole point. Finally the outbox relays its recorded event to the Kafka payment-events topic for the notification, analytics, and reconciliation consumers.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I design a payment gateway, I start with the request path and the correctness guarantees. Requests enter through an API gateway that does TLS termination, authentication, and rate limiting, and behind it the payment service is stateless and horizontally scaled so any instance can serve any request. The most important property is idempotency: the client sends an idempotency key, I store it in Redis mapped to the result, and if the same key arrives again from a retry I return the stored result instead of moving money twice. In my project this is exactly what stopped Rajesh being debited twice when his phone retried a request.

Because moving money spans multiple services, I do not rely on a single database transaction. I use the Saga pattern, which is a sequence of local transactions where each step has a compensating action. I debit the sender, then credit the receiver, then record settlement, and if crediting the receiver fails I run the compensation to re-credit the sender, so the system is never left with money missing. I demonstrated this in code: when the credit step throws, the service immediately re-credits the sender and the balances end up unchanged.

To tell the rest of the system what happened without coupling, I use the transactional outbox pattern. In the same transaction that commits the payment, I insert an event into an outbox table, and a relay publishes it to a Kafka topic. This avoids the dual-write problem because the event is published only if the payment committed. Consumers then react asynchronously: one sends the SMS and email, one updates analytics, and one does end-of-day reconciliation. This gives me strong consistency for the money movement and eventual consistency for notifications, which is the correct trade-off because a slightly delayed SMS is acceptable but a lost debit is not.

For scale and reliability, I shard PostgreSQL by account id and use read replicas for heavy reporting, I cache idempotency keys and rate-limit counters in Redis, and I wrap every downstream call in a circuit breaker with retry so a transient failure does not cascade. Finally I make the whole thing observable with Prometheus and Grafana metrics, structured logs in ELK, distributed tracing with correlation ids through Jaeger, and PagerDuty alerts when the ninety-ninth percentile latency or the error rate crosses a threshold. That combination of idempotency, Saga-based consistency, event-driven decoupling, resilience, and observability is what makes a payment gateway safe to run at scale.
